edges.description: Abnormal Cav1.4 channel function impairs calcium-dependent signaling at rod and cone photoreceptor synapses.
CACNA1F-associated retinal dysfunction is linked to axial myopia and astigmatism, but the intervening ocular-growth mechanism is unresolved.
CACNA1F-associated disease includes foveal hypoplasia, but the developmental steps from altered Cav1.4 function to abnormal foveal architecture are unknown.
Fundus hypopigmentation and iris transillumination distinguish many AIED presentations from overlapping CSNB2A, but the molecular intermediates are unknown.
Photoreceptor-to-bipolar synaptic dysfunction impairs rod- and cone-mediated retinal function and produces the characteristic visual phenotype.
The retinal channelopathy phenotype includes color-vision defects.
Early degraded retinal input is associated with nystagmus, but the developmental intermediates between impaired visual function and the ocular motor phenotype are unresolved.
The retinal visual-function phenotype includes reduced acuity.
The retinal signal defect manifests as impaired dark adaptation.

edges.description: Impaired scotopic retinal function manifests clinically as nyctalopia.
The ocular-growth phenotype includes progressive axial myopia.
Choroidal thinning co-occurred with high myopia in two patients and is modeled as a possible downstream structural consequence of abnormal ocular growth; the intervening mechanism was not tested.
The developmental retinal abnormality is observed clinically as foveal hypoplasia.
Ocular hypopigmentation is visible as a blonde or hypopigmented fundus.
Reduced iris pigmentation can produce a transillumination defect.
The retinal signal-transmission defect is measured clinically as the characteristic abnormal electroretinogram.
